en: Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.1 (SN 38.1, PTS SN iv 251) 1. Jambukhādakavagga Nibbānapañhāsutta (The Discourse on the Question on Nibbāna) At Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Jambukhādaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their courteous greetings and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it has been said: ‘Nibbāna, Nibbāna. In what way, venerable sir, is the term ‘Nibbāna’ used? “Jambukhādaka, when a bhikkhu is liberated through the destruction of craving, he is called ‘one who has attained Nibbāna in this very life. It is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that the term ‘Nibbāna’ is used. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that in this very life one is declared by the Blessed One to be one who has attained Nibbāna? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that in this very life one is declared by the Blessed One to be one who has attained Nibbāna. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all sufferings? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all sufferings. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all taints? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all taints. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all fetters? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all fetters. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all bonds? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all bonds. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all attachments? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all attachments.

“But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all cravings? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all cravings. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all conceits? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all conceits. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all obsessions? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all obsessions. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all corruptions? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all corruptions. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all defilements? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all defilements. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all fermentations? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all fermentations. “But, venerable sir, how does one know, how does one see, so that one is completely freed from all cankers? “When, Jambukhādaka, a bhikkhu sees as it really is with correct wisdom: ‘This is suffering,’ and ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ and ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ and ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—it is in this way, Jambukhādaka, that one knows, it is in this way that one sees, so that one is completely freed from all cankers. When this was said, the wanderer Jambukhādaka said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at the village of Nālakagāma.
Then the wanderer Jambukhādaka approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the wanderer Jambukhādaka said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Friend Sāriputta, it is said, ‘Nibbāna, Nibbāna.
What now, friend, is Nibbāna?
“Friend, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—that, friend, is Nibbāna.”
“This is called Nibbāna.
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the realization of this Nibbāna?
“There is indeed, friend, a path; there is a way for the realization of this Nibbāna.”
“But what, friends, is the path, what is the way for the realization of this Nibbāna?
“Friends, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the realization of this Nibbāna; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
“This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the realization of this Nibbāna.
“Excellent, friend, is the path; excellent is the way for the realization of this Nibbāna.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.”
First.

Jambukhādakavagga
The Discourse on the Question Concerning Arahantship:
“Friend Sāriputta, ‘arahantship, arahantship’ is said.
What, friend, is arahantship?”
“Friend, the destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, and the destruction of delusion—
this is called ‘arahantship.
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the realization of this arahantship?”
“There is, friend, a path, there is a way for the realization of this arahantship.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the realization of this arahantship?
“Friend, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path that is the way for the realization of this arahantship; namely:”
“Right view ... right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the realization of this arahantship.
“Excellent, friend, is the path; excellent is the way for the realization of this arahantship.”
“Enough, friend Sāriputta, with diligence!
This is the second [sutta]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.3 (SN 38.3, PTS SN iv 252)
1. The Chapter on Jambukhādaka. The Discourse on the Questions of the Proponent of Dhamma:
“Who, friend Sāriputta, are the proponents of Dhamma in the world? Who in the world are those who have practiced rightly? Who in the world are the Well-Gone Ones?”
“Friends, those who teach the Dhamma for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—they are the speakers of Dhamma in the world.
Those, friends, who have practiced for the abandoning of lust, for the abandoning of hatred, and for the abandoning of delusion—they are those who have practiced well in the world.
Those, friends, for whom lust has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more subject to future arising;”
"Hatred has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future;
delusion has been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future—these are the Sugatas in the world.
"But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion?"
“There is, friend, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion?
“Friend, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion; that is to say:”
“Right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the abandoning of this lust, hatred, and delusion.”
"Enough, friend Sāriputta, of diligence.
This is the third [sutta]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 38.4 (SN 38.4, PTS SN iv 253).
1. The Chapter on Jambukhādaka.
“For what purpose, friend Sāriputta, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?”
“Friend, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One for the sake of the full understanding of suffering.
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the full understanding of this suffering?
“There is indeed, friend, a path; there is a way for the full understanding of this suffering.”
“But what, friends, is the path, what is the way for the full understanding of this suffering?
“Friends, it is precisely this Noble Eightfold Path for the full understanding of this suffering; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.”
“This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the full understanding of this suffering.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the full understanding of this suffering.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 38.5 (SN 38.5, PTS SN iv 254) 1.
Jambukhādakavagga
“Friend Sāriputta, it is said, ‘one who has attained consolation, one who has attained consolation.
To what extent, friend, is one said to have attained consolation?”

“Friend, when a bhikkhu understands, as they truly are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, to that extent, friend, he has attained consolation.
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the realization of this consolation?
“There is indeed, friend, a path; there is a way for the realization of this consolation.”
“But what, friends, is the path, what is the way for the realization of this consolation?
“Friends, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path for the realization of this consolation; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.”
“This, friend, is the path, this is the way for the realization of this consolation.
“Excellent, friend, is the path; excellent is the way for the realization of this consolation.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.”
The Fifth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.6 (SN 38.6, PTS SN iv 254) 1.
Jambukhādakavagga (The Chapter on Jambukhādaka)
“Friend Sāriputta, it is said: ‘One who has attained supreme consolation, one who has attained supreme consolation.
In what way, friend, is one said to have attained supreme consolation?”

“Friend, when a bhikkhu, having understood as they really are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact, becomes liberated through non-clinging,
to this extent, friend, he has attained supreme consolation.”
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the realization of this supreme consolation?
“There is indeed, friend, a path, there is a way for the realization of this supreme consolation.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the realization of this supreme consolation?”
“Friends, this very Noble Eightfold Path is for the realization of this supreme consolation; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the realization of this supreme consolation.”
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this practice for the realization of this supreme consolation.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.
The sixth.

“‘Feeling, feeling,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said.
What now, friend, is feeling?
“There are these three feelings, friend.”
Which three?
Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—
these, friend, are the three feelings.”
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the full understanding of these three feelings?
“There is indeed, friend, a path, there is a way for the full understanding of these three feelings.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the full understanding of these three feelings?”
“Indeed, friend, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path for the full understanding of these three kinds of feeling, namely:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
This, friend, is the path, this is the way for the full understanding of these three kinds of feeling.”
“Friends, the path is auspicious, the practice is auspicious for the full understanding of these three feelings.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, for diligence.
The seventh.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.8 (SN 38.8, PTS SN iv 256) 1. Jambukhādakavagga Āsavapañhāsutta (The Discourse on the Question on the Taints) Then the wanderer Jambukhādaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation and cordial greetings, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? "It is, Jambukhādaka, because they have not abandoned the taints that lead to rebirth, the taints that lead to old age, the taints that lead to death, the taints that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; it is for this reason that some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause, what is the reason, why some beings here do attain final Nibbāna in this very life? "It is, Jambukhādaka, because they have abandoned the taints that lead to rebirth, the taints that lead to old age, the taints that lead to death, the taints that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; it is for this reason that some beings here do attain final Nibbāna in this very life. When this was said, the wanderer Jambukhādaka said to the Blessed One: "Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what has been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who is lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
“‘Taint, taint,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said.
What now, friend, is a taint?
“There are, friend, three taints.”
“The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance—
these, friends, are the three taints.
“But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of these taints?”
“There is, friend, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of these taints.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the abandoning of these taints?
“This very Noble Eightfold Path, friend, is the way for the abandoning of these taints; that is to say:”
“Right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of these taints.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the abandoning of these taints.”
“Enough, friend Sāriputta, with diligence!
This is the eighth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 38.9 (SN 38.9, PTS SN iv 256).
1. The Chapter on Jambukhādaka. The Discourse on the Question on Ignorance:
“‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said.”
“What, friends, is ignorance? “That which, friends,

is lack of knowledge regarding suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the origin of suffering, lack of knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering, and lack of knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering—
this, friends, is called ignorance.”
“But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of this ignorance?
“There is indeed, friends, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of this ignorance.
“But what, friends, is that path, what is that way for the abandoning of this ignorance?”
“Friends, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path for the abandoning of this ignorance; that is to say:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of this ignorance.”
“Venerable friend, this path is auspicious; this practice is auspicious for the abandoning of this ignorance.
And it is enough, venerable Sāriputta, for diligence.
The ninth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.10 (SN 38.10, PTS SN iv 257) 1.
Jambukhādakavagga The Discourse on the Question on Craving (Taṇhāpañhāsutta)
“‘Craving, craving,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said.
What now, friend, is craving?
“There are these three kinds of craving, friend.”
“Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence,
and craving for non-existence— these, friend, are the three kinds of craving. “But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of these cravings?”
“There is, friend, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of these cravings.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the abandoning of these cravings?
“This very Noble Eightfold Path, friend, is the way for the abandoning of these cravings; that is to say:”
“Right view... [and so on] ...right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of these cravings.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the abandoning of these cravings.”
“Enough, friend Sāriputta, with diligence!
Tenth. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 38.11 (SN 38.11, PTS SN iv 257)
1. The Chapter on Jambukhādaka The Discourse on the Questions on the Floods “Friend Sāriputta, ‘the flood, the flood’ is said.”
“What, friends, is the flood?
“Friends, there are these four floods:
the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.”
“Friends, these indeed are the four floods.
“But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of these floods?
“There is indeed, friends, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of these floods.”
“But what, friends, is the path, what is the way for the abandoning of these floods?
“Friends, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path for the abandoning of these floods; that is to say:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.”
“This, friend, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of these floods.
“Excellent, friend, is the path; excellent is the way for the abandoning of these floods.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, for diligence.”
Eleventh.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 38.12 (SN 38.12, PTS SN iv 258) 1.
Jambukhādakavagga (The Chapter with Jambukhādaka)
The Discourse on the Question of Clinging:
“Friend Sāriputta, it is said: ‘clinging, clinging.
Now, friend, what is clinging?”
“Friends, there are these four kinds of clinging.
Sensual clinging, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self—
these, friends, are the four kinds of clinging.”
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the abandoning of these clingings?
“There is indeed, friend, a path, there is a way for the abandoning of these clingings.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the abandoning of these clingings?”
“Indeed, friend, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the abandoning of these clingings; that is to say:
right view ... [and so on] ... right concentration.
This, friend, is the path, this is the way for the abandoning of these clingings.”
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this practice for the abandoning of these forms of clinging.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.
The twelfth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.13 (SN 38.13, PTS SN iv 258) 1. Jambukhādakavagga Bhavapañhāsutta: The Discourse on the Question on Existence Then the wanderer Jambukhādaka approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, it has been said: 'Existence, existence. In what way, venerable sir, is there existence? "Jambukhādaka, when there is feeling, through the arising of feeling there is the arising of existence; through the cessation of feeling there is the cessation of existence. "But, venerable sir, how does feeling arise? From what source does feeling come? "When there is contact, Jambukhādaka, from the arising of contact there is the arising of feeling; from the cessation of contact there is the cessation of feeling. "But, venerable sir, how does contact arise? From what source does contact come? "When there is name-and-form, Jambukhādaka, from the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of contact; from the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of contact. "But, venerable sir, how does name-and-form arise? From what source does name-and-form come? "When there is consciousness, Jambukhādaka, from the arising of consciousness there is the arising of name-and-form; from the cessation of consciousness there is the cessation of name-and-form. "But, venerable sir, how does consciousness arise? From what source does consciousness come? "When there are volitional formations, Jambukhādaka, from the arising of volitional formations there is the arising of consciousness; from the cessation of volitional formations there is the cessation of consciousness. "But, venerable sir, how do volitional formations arise? From what source do volitional formations come? "When there is ignorance, Jambukhādaka, from the arising of ignorance there is the arising of volitional formations; from the cessation of ignorance there is the cessation of volitional formations. "It is, Jambukhādaka, by this method that these volitional formations are conditioned by ignorance. "Thus, venerable sir, for one who does not see the Dhamma as it really is, ignorance is the cause; from ignorance as a cause, volitional formations come to be; from volitional formations as a cause, consciousness comes to be; from consciousness as a cause, name-and-form comes to be; from name-and-form as a cause, contact comes to be; from contact as a cause, feeling comes to be; from feeling as a cause, existence comes to be; from existence as a cause, birth comes to be; from birth as a cause, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. "But, venerable sir, for one who sees the Dhamma as it really is, ignorance ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. When this was said, the wanderer Jambukhādaka said to the Blessed One: "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... [as in standard formula]... May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last."
“‘Becoming, becoming,’ friend Sāriputta, it is said.
What now, friend, is becoming?
“Friend, there are these three kinds of becoming.”
“Sensual existence, form existence, and formless existence—
these, friends, are the three kinds of existence.
“But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the full understanding of these existences?”
“There is, friend, a path, there is a way for the full understanding of these states of existence.
“But what, friend, is that path, what is that way for the full understanding of these states of existence?
“This very Noble Eightfold Path, friend, is for the full understanding of these states of existence; that is to say:”
“Right view... right concentration.
This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the full understanding of these states of existence.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the full understanding of these states of existence.”
“And enough, friend Sāriputta, with diligence.
The Thirteenth [Discourse]. Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.14 (SN 38.14, PTS SN iv 259)
1. The Chapter on Jambukhādaka.
Discourse on the Question of Suffering:
“Friend Sāriputta, it is said: ‘Suffering, suffering.’”
“Friend, what now is suffering?
“Friend, there are these three kinds of suffering:
the suffering of suffering, the suffering of formations, and the suffering of change.”
“Friend, these are the three kinds of suffering.
“But, friend, is there a path, is there a way for the full understanding of these kinds of suffering?
“There is, friend, a path; there is a way for the full understanding of these kinds of suffering.”
“But what, friends, is the path, what is the way for the full understanding of these forms of suffering?
“Friends, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path for the full understanding of these forms of suffering; that is to say:
right view … right concentration.”
“This, friends, is the path, this is the way for the full understanding of these forms of suffering.
“Excellent, friend, is this path; excellent is this way for the full understanding of these forms of suffering.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.”
The Fourteenth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.15 (SN 38.15, PTS SN iv 259) 1.
Jambukhādakavagga
The Discourse on the Question of Identity:
“Friend Sāriputta, it is said, ‘identity, identity.
Now, friend, what is identity?”
“Friends, these five aggregates of clinging have been called ‘personality’ by the Blessed One; that is to say:
the form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the volitional formations aggregate of clinging, and the consciousness aggregate of clinging.
These, friends, are the five aggregates of clinging that have been called ‘personality’ by the Blessed One.”
“But, friends, is there a path, is there a way for the full understanding of this personal existence?
“There is indeed, friends, a path, there is a way for the full understanding of this personal existence.
“But what, friends, is that path, what is that way for the full understanding of this personal existence?”
“Indeed, friend, it is this very Noble Eightfold Path that leads to the full understanding of this personal existence, namely:
right view … [and so on] … right concentration.
This, friend, is the path, this is the way, for the full understanding of this personal existence.”
“Friend, the path is auspicious, the practice is auspicious, for the full understanding of this personal existence.
And it is enough, friend Sāriputta, to be diligent.
The fifteenth.

Saṁyutta Nikāya 38.16 Jambukhādakavagga The Discourse on the Question on What is Difficult to Do “Venerable sir, what is difficult to do? “Householder, it is difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’; ‘this is the origin of suffering’; ‘this is the cessation of suffering’; and ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized, and who does not live having made the four foundations of mindfulness their support. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized, and who does not live having made the four foundations of mindfulness their support, and who does not develop the seven factors of enlightenment. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized, and who does not live having made the four foundations of mindfulness their support, and who does not develop the seven factors of enlightenment, and who does not realize the four paths and the four fruits. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized, and who does not live having made the four foundations of mindfulness their support, and who does not develop the seven factors of enlightenment, and who does not realize the four paths and the four fruits, and who does not attain final Nibbāna in this very life. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized, and who does not live having made the four foundations of mindfulness their support, and who does not develop the seven factors of enlightenment, and who does not realize the four paths and the four fruits, and who does not attain final Nibbāna in this very life, and who does not attain final Nibbāna in the interval between lives, nor at the time of death, nor upon rebirth, nor after having traversed some part of the journey. “But, venerable sir, what is even more difficult to do than that? “Householder, it is even more difficult to do that which is not done by one who has not abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, and who does not understand as they really are: ‘This is suffering’... ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ and who does not realize the four noble truths as they have been realized, and who does not live having made the four foundations of mindfulness their support, and who does not develop the seven factors of enlightenment, and who does not realize the four paths and the four fruits, and who does not attain final Nibbāna in this very life, nor in the interval between lives, nor at the time of death, nor upon rebirth, nor after having traversed some part of the journey, and who does not attain final Nibbāna after having reached the end of the journey.

“Friend Sāriputta, what indeed is difficult to do in this Dhamma and Discipline?
“Going forth, friend, is difficult to do in this Dhamma and Discipline.
“But for one who has gone forth, friend, what is difficult to do?”
“Friend, it is difficult for one who has gone forth to find delight.
“But friend, what is difficult for one who finds delight?
“Friend, it is difficult for one who finds delight to practice in accordance with the Dhamma.”
“But how long, friend, before a bhikkhu who practices in accordance with the Dhamma becomes an arahant?
“Not long, friend.
(The sixteenth.)
The Saṃyutta on Jambukhādaka is complete.
Its summary verse:
Nibbāna and Arahantship.
What is the purpose of one who speaks according to the Dhamma?
[It is] for the sake of inspiration, supreme inspiration,
feeling, the taints, and ignorance.
Craving, the flood, clinging,
existence, suffering, and identity—
these are difficult to overcome in this Dhamma and Discipline.
